goals.goal: Which tokio Cargo features do I need for #[tokio::main] with the multi-threaded runtime, and what does the full feature do?

nuggets.text: The tokio feature flag "macros" enables the #[tokio::main] and #[tokio::test] attributes.
The tokio feature flag "rt-multi-thread" enables the multi-threaded, work-stealing scheduler.
The tokio feature flag "rt" enables tokio::spawn and the current-thread scheduler.
Enabling tokio's "full" feature turns on all features: tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }.
#[tokio::main] uses the multi-threaded runtime flavor by default, which requires the rt-multi-thread feature.
#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")] selects the single-threaded current_thread runtime.

goals.goal: How do I enable #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] in serde, and what do the Serialize and Deserialize trait methods look like?

nuggets.text: The Serialize and Deserialize derive macros are only available if serde is built with features = ["derive"].
Serialize has one required method: fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error> where S: Serializer.
Deserialize<'de> has one required method: fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error> where D: Deserializer<'de>.
Serde is built on Rust's trait system rather than runtime reflection or runtime type information.
Serde separates data structures (implementing Serialize/Deserialize) from data formats, so any supported structure works with any supported format such as JSON, TOML or YAML.

goals.goal: Which async runtime does reqwest's Client need, and which Cargo features are required for .json(), .form() and the blocking API?

nuggets.text: The reqwest::Client is asynchronous and requires Tokio.
The reqwest "json" feature is required for RequestBuilder::json (JSON body serialization/deserialization).
The reqwest "form" feature is required for RequestBuilder::form (form data serialization).
The reqwest "blocking" feature provides the blocking client API (reqwest::blocking).
By default a reqwest Client follows HTTP redirects with a maximum redirect chain of 10 hops.
For multiple requests, reqwest recommends creating one Client and reusing it to benefit from keep-alive connection pooling.

goals.goal: How do I define command-line arguments with clap's derive API, and which feature flag must be enabled?

nuggets.text: The clap "derive" feature enables the custom derive (#[derive(Parser)]); it can be added with `cargo add clap --features derive`.
A clap derive CLI is defined as a struct annotated with #[derive(Parser, Debug)] and parsed by calling Args::parse() (use clap::Parser).
Struct fields are configured with #[arg(short, long)] attributes, and default_value_t = 1 sets a default value for a field such as count: u8.
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)] on the struct sets up version and about info for the generated help.
clap's default features are std, color, help, usage, error-context and suggestions.
The clap "env" feature turns on the usage of environment variables during parsing.

goals.goal: How do I attach context to errors with anyhow, and how do I use anyhow in a no_std crate?

nuggets.text: anyhow::Result<T> is equivalent to Result<T, anyhow::Error>, where anyhow::Error is a trait-object based error type.
The anyhow::Context trait (use anyhow::Context) provides the .context() method, with .with_context(|| ...) for lazily built messages, on Result.
When an anyhow error with context is printed, the outermost context is shown first, followed by "Caused by:" and the lower level causes.
The anyhow! macro builds a one-off anyhow::Error from a message with string interpolation, and bail! is a shorthand for returning Err(anyhow!(...)) early.
To use anyhow in no_std mode, disable the default "std" feature (default-features = false); a global allocator is required.
With Rust 1.65 or newer, anyhow captures a backtrace, shown when RUST_BACKTRACE=1 (panics and errors) or RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1 (errors only) is set.

goals.goal: How do I compile and reuse a regex with Rust's regex crate, and what regex features does the crate not support?

nuggets.text: Regex::new compiles a regular expression; compilation is somewhat expensive and not automatically cached, so compile once and reuse it rather than in a loop.
The regex docs recommend std::sync::LazyLock (or the once_cell crate) to hold a static Regex so it compiles only once in helper functions.
The regex crate does not support look-around or backreferences.
All regex searches have worst case O(m * n) time, where m is proportional to the regex size and n to the haystack size.
Regex::is_match reports whether a match exists, Regex::find returns the byte offsets of a match, and Regex::captures returns a Captures with capture group offsets.
regex-lite is a standalone zero-dependency, simpler alternative to regex that favors compile time and binary size over Unicode support and performance.

goals.goal: How do I use rayon parallel iterators and control the number of threads in its global thread pool?

nuggets.text: Import the rayon prelude with use rayon::prelude::* to get traits that provide par_iter and other parallel iterator methods.
rayon::ThreadPoolBuilder can create custom thread pools or customize the global rayon thread pool.
If num_threads is 0 or not called, rayon chooses the thread count from the RAYON_NUM_THREADS environment variable if set, otherwise the number of logical CPUs.
rayon::join takes two closures, potentially runs them in parallel, and returns a pair of their results (RA, RB).
rayon::join uses work stealing on a fixed pool of worker threads and only runs code in parallel when there are idle CPUs.
Rayon guarantees data-race free executions.

goals.goal: How do I record spans and events with the tracing crate, and how do I install a subscriber in an executable?

nuggets.text: A tracing span represents a period of time with a beginning and end; Span::enter returns an RAII guard that exits the span when dropped.
Holding the Span::enter guard across an .await point in async code may produce incorrect traces.
The #[instrument] attribute creates and enters a span named after the function on each call and records the arguments as fields using fmt::Debug.
Events are recorded with the event! macro, e.g. event!(Level::INFO, "something happened"); an Event may occur inside a span.
The tracing crate contains no Subscriber implementations; executables must install one, e.g. with tracing::subscriber::set_global_default.
Libraries should not call set_global_default(); libraries should only link the tracing crate and use its macros.
